headings.title: Introduction and Purpose of Nutritional Assessment
headings.content: Nutritional assessment is a comprehensive, systematic method used to evaluate the nutritional status of individuals. In clinical settings, it serves as a critical baseline to detect hidden deficits, chronic excesses, or metabolic imbalances before severe pathological consequences manifest. The primary goal is not merely to record body weight, but to interpret a constellation of findings that indicate how well the body ingests, absorbs, and utilizes dietary nutrients. By identifying vulnerabilities early, healthcare teams can prevent secondary complications during illness or surgery.

headings.title: The ABCD Approach to Assessment Data
headings.content:
Clinical evaluation relies on four distinct categories of data, universally known as the **ABCD** framework. Integrating these four dimensions creates a complete physiological and dietary profile.

- **Anthropometric measurements**: Physical dimensions including height, weight, body mass index, and skinfold thickness.
- **Biochemical indices**: Laboratory values such as serum albumin, prealbumin, hemoglobin, and electrolyte panels.
- **Clinical examination**: Physical inspection focusing on tissues with rapid cell turnover, like skin, hair, nails, and oral mucosa.
- **Dietary history**: Detailed records of past food intake, eating patterns, swallowing difficulties, and food access.

headings.title: Clinical Significance in Nursing Practice
headings.content: Every patient admitted to a health facility undergoes initial observation, yet nutritional status is frequently overlooked until visible wasting occurs. Malnourished patients face extended hospital stays, impaired wound healing, higher infection rates, and reduced tolerance to pharmacological therapies. Recognizing subtle shifts in dietary intake allows nurses to advocate for timely dietary interventions, support metabolic recovery, and reduce overall hospital morbidity.

headings.title: Identifying Malnutrition and Nutritional Risk
headings.content: Malnutrition presents in multiple forms, encompassing both undernutrition (such as marasmus and kwashiorkor) and overnutrition (obesity and micronutrient toxicity). Nutritional risk refers to the likelihood that a patient's current condition or medical treatment will worsen their nutritional state. Identifying this risk requires looking beyond current weight to factor in involuntary weight loss percentages, recent disease severity, and anticipated periods of fasting or metabolic stress.

headings.title: The Role of the Nurse in Nutritional Screening
headings.content: Nutritional screening is a rapid, straightforward process performed upon admission to flag individuals who are malnourished or at risk. While a full assessment is detailed and often conducted by a multidisciplinary team or dietitian, the nurse acts as the first line of defense by executing the initial screen. Using validated tools like the **Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST)** or **Nutritional Risk Screening (NRS-2000)**, nurses gather quick metrics on weight history, body mass index, and acute illness effect to trigger formal nutritional care pathways.
